COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- Sri Lanka President Mahinda Rajapaksa claimed Friday there was "a conspiracy with certain international forces" to belittle his government's military victories against Tamil Tiger rebels. Sri Lankan army troops have had there most decisive victories against the Tamil Tigers in recent weeks. The aim of these conspirators, he said in an address to the nation, "is to level unfounded charges against the army commander who works with greatest dedication to achieve these victories." He also used the address to formally announce the recapture of the northern town of Elephant Pass, the point at which mainland Sri Lanka links to the northern Jaffna peninsula. It had remained in rebel hands for over nine years. The recapture enable the government to use the A-9 highway linking the mainland to the peninsula to move troops and supplies. Until now it was done either by air or by sea. Rajapaksa's remarks came amid mounting attacks on the media. On Tuesday a group armed with rifles, pistols and grenades attacked the country's most popular privately owned television channel MTV. The main control room equipment costing more than $ 1.7 million was damaged. On Thursday, Lasantha Wickrematunga, chief editor of The Sunday Leader, a newspaper which had exposed corruption and criticized aspects of ongoing military operations, was shot dead. Earlier Friday, the leader of the main opposition United National Party (UNP), Ranil Wickremasinghe, accused military and security officials of the attacks, saying the government could not control them. "Armed forces members are shocked about these incidents. The armed forces says due to the activities of few intelligence sections, the reputation of the country is being ruined. That is the team which the government has no control of," he told parliament. Rajapaksa said there were efforts to belittle military victories "to turn the attention of the people to other directions." He said such "conspiracies arise when a country moves ahead without giving in to external pressures." He added "one must not mistake these conspiracies as being against me or my government. This is a conspiracy against the entire country by those who have been driven to fear due to the successes of our security forces." Meanwhile, fighting in northern Sri Lanka between government and rebel forces escalated on several fronts Friday, while Tamil Tiger rebels killed seven people in a roadside bombing. Three members of the Sri Lankan air force and four civilians died when rebels exploded a claymore landmine in the village of Morawewa, near the northeastern port city of Trincomalee, police said. The strategic port town is located about 240km (150 miles) north of the capital, Colombo. Friday's incident came as troops pursued their military campaign in the northern Wanni region to recapture remaining rebel strongholds, military sources said. Government troops were said to be meeting fierce resistance as they advanced on the Tamil stronghold of Mullaitivu and a naval blockade remained in the northeastern seas. The 25-year long civil war has left more than 65,000 people dead. The U.S. State Department has designated the Tamil Tigers a terrorist organization.

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- On Friday, Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa alleged that "certain international forces" had joined together in "a conspiracy" designed to diminish the recent military triumphs his administration had secured over the Tamil Tiger rebels. Over the past several weeks, Sri Lankan forces have scored their most significant successes against the insurgents.

Speaking to the nation, Rajapaksa declared that these plotters intended "to level unfounded charges against the army commander who works with greatest dedication to achieve these victories."

During the same address, he officially confirmed that government forces had retaken Elephant Pass, the strategic northern town that serves as the connection between Sri Lanka's mainland and the Jaffna peninsula in the north. The rebels had controlled this location for more than nine years. With its recapture, the government can now transport soldiers and provisions along the A-9 highway that connects the mainland with the peninsula—a route previously accessible only by air or sea.

The president's statements followed a series of intensifying assaults targeting journalists and news outlets. On Tuesday, an armed group carrying rifles, pistols, and grenades stormed MTV, the nation's leading private television station, causing more than $1.7 million in damage to its primary control room equipment. Then on Thursday, gunmen fatally shot Lasantha Wickrematunga, who edited The Sunday Leader—a publication known for uncovering corruption and questioning certain elements of the military campaigns.

Earlier that same Friday, Ranil Wickremasinghe, who heads the leading opposition United National Party (UNP), placed blame for the attacks on military and security personnel, contending that the government had lost control over them. Addressing parliament, he stated: "Armed forces members are shocked about these incidents. The armed forces says due to the activities of few intelligence sections, the reputation of the country is being ruined. That is the team which the government has no control of."

Rajapaksa maintained that attempts to downplay the military's accomplishments were meant "to turn the attention of the people to other directions." According to him, such "conspiracies arise when a country moves ahead without giving in to external pressures." He continued: "one must not mistake these conspiracies as being against me or my government. This is a conspiracy against the entire country by those who have been driven to fear due to the successes of our security forces."

At the same time, combat between government and rebel forces intensified across multiple areas of northern Sri Lanka on Friday. In one incident, Tamil Tiger fighters detonated a roadside bomb that took seven lives. Police reported that four civilians and three members of the Sri Lankan air force were killed when the rebels set off a claymore landmine in Morawewa, a village situated close to Trincomalee, a port city in the northeast. This important harbor town lies roughly 240km (150 miles) to the north of Colombo, the capital.

Military sources indicated that Friday's attack coincided with an ongoing offensive by government troops throughout the northern Wanni region aimed at seizing the rebels' remaining bases. As soldiers pushed toward Mullaitivu, a Tamil stronghold, they reportedly faced intense opposition, while a naval blockade continued along the northeastern coastline.

The civil war, which has now spanned 25 years, has claimed the lives of over 65,000 people. The Tamil Tigers have been officially classified as a terrorist organization by the U.S. State Department.

Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa alleged that international forces were conspiring to undermine his government's military successes against the Tamil Tiger rebels. His comments reflected the government's growing confidence following a series of significant battlefield gains, while simultaneously suggesting that external powers were working to diminish these achievements.

## The Recapture of Elephant Pass

The government formally announced the recapture of Elephant Pass, a strategically vital town that links mainland Sri Lanka to the Jaffna peninsula. The town had been held by rebel forces for over nine years, making its recovery a symbolic and practical turning point in the long-running conflict.

The military significance of this victory cannot be overstated. The recapture allows the government to use the A-9 highway to transport troops and supplies by land, rather than relying solely on air or sea routes as had previously been necessary. This overland access substantially improves the government's logistical capabilities and strengthens its position in the ongoing campaign against the rebels.

## Escalating Attacks on the Media

However, Rajapaksa's remarks coincided with a troubling escalation of attacks on the media. These included an armed assault on the MTV television channel, as well as the fatal shooting of Lasantha Wickrematunga, editor of the *Sunday Leader*. The killing of a prominent journalist, in particular, drew widespread attention and raised serious concerns about press freedom and the safety of media professionals in the country.

## Opposition Accusations

In the wake of these attacks, opposition United National Party (UNP) leader Ranil Wickremasinghe accused military and security officials of carrying out the assaults. He claimed that the government had lost control over certain intelligence sections, suggesting that elements within the security apparatus were operating beyond official oversight. These accusations added a further dimension to the political tensions surrounding the government's military campaign and its relationship with the press.

# President Rajapaksa Alleges International Conspiracy Amid Military Gains and Media Crackdown

Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa delivered a nationally televised address on Friday in which he simultaneously celebrated a significant military victory and issued a defiant response to mounting international criticism of his government's conduct in the ongoing conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).

In his remarks, Rajapaksa formally announced that government forces had recaptured Elephant Pass, the strategically vital northern town that connects the Jaffna Peninsula to the rest of the island. The narrow land corridor had remained under rebel control for nine years, serving as a critical supply and defensive position for the Tamil Tigers. Its recapture represents a major strategic and symbolic triumph for the military, which has made steady territorial advances against the separatist group in recent months.

However, the President's speech was equally notable for its combative tone toward foreign observers and critics. Rajapaksa alleged that an international conspiracy was underway to discredit the achievements of his armed forces and to undermine the government's campaign against the rebels. He suggested that external actors were seeking to tarnish the reputation of the military at precisely the moment when it appeared poised to achieve a decisive victory in the decades-long civil war.

## A Climate of Fear for Journalists

The President's address came against a troubling backdrop of escalating violence directed at the country's media. In recent days, a Sri Lankan television station was subjected to a violent assault by armed attackers, raising alarm among press freedom advocates. Even more disturbing was the fatal shooting of a prominent newspaper editor known for his sharp criticism of the government's military operations and its handling of the war.

These incidents have intensified fears that independent journalism in Sri Lanka is being systematically suppressed. Media organizations and human rights groups have expressed grave concern that the targeting of outlets and individuals critical of the government reflects a broader pattern of intimidation designed to silence dissent during a sensitive phase of the conflict.

## Opposition Accusations and Questions of Accountability

Opposition leaders have responded to the violence with pointed accusations, alleging that government security forces may have orchestrated or facilitated the attacks. Such claims strike at the heart of questions surrounding state accountability, suggesting that elements within the government apparatus could be directly involved in the assault on press freedom.

The government has strongly denied any involvement in the attacks. Nevertheless, the convergence of military triumphalism, allegations of foreign conspiracy, and a deteriorating environment for the free press has drawn significant scrutiny both domestically and abroad.

As the military closes in on the remaining rebel-held territory, observers warn that the shrinking space for independent reporting could obscure the human cost of the conflict and prevent meaningful oversight of the actions of both the state and the insurgents. The situation underscores the difficult balance between national security imperatives and the fundamental democratic values of transparency, accountability, and freedom of expression.

# Colombo: The Vibrant Heart of Sri Lanka

Colombo stands as the largest city and commercial capital of Sri Lanka, a beautiful island nation located in South Asia. Situated on the western coast of the country, this bustling metropolis serves as the economic and cultural center of the nation, blending rich history with modern development.

## A City of History

Colombo has a fascinating past shaped by centuries of trade and colonial influence. Over the years, the city was controlled by Portuguese, Dutch, and British powers, each leaving their mark on its architecture, culture, and identity. Today, visitors can still see remnants of this colonial heritage throughout the city, particularly in areas like the Fort district.

## Attractions and Landmarks

The city offers numerous attractions for both tourists and locals alike. The Gangaramaya Temple is one of the most important Buddhist temples in Sri Lanka, showcasing intricate architecture and religious significance. The Galle Face Green, a scenic ocean-side promenade, provides a perfect spot for relaxation and enjoying beautiful sunsets over the Indian Ocean.

Other notable sites include the National Museum of Colombo, the vibrant Pettah Market, and the modern Lotus Tower, which has become an iconic feature of the city's skyline.

## A Blend of Cultures

One of Colombo's most striking features is its cultural diversity. The city is home to people of various ethnicities and religions, including Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and Christians. This diversity is reflected in the city's temples, mosques, churches, and the wide array of delicious cuisine available throughout its streets.

## Economic Significance

As Sri Lanka's commercial hub, Colombo plays a crucial role in the nation's economy. The city hosts the country's main seaport, numerous businesses, financial institutions, and government offices. Its strategic location along important maritime trade routes has historically made it a significant center for commerce.

## Conclusion

Colombo represents the dynamic spirit of Sri Lanka, combining ancient traditions with contemporary progress. Whether exploring its historical sites, enjoying its culinary delights, or experiencing its vibrant street life, visitors to Colombo are sure to find a city full of energy, color, and charm.

# Sri Lankan President Alleges International Conspiracy Amid Military Gains Against Tamil Tigers

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has accused unnamed international forces of orchestrating a conspiracy against his government, claiming that outside powers are working to undermine the military's recent battlefield successes against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).

Speaking to supporters, Rajapaksa suggested that international criticism of his government's conduct in the ongoing civil war was part of a coordinated effort to deny Sri Lanka a decisive victory over the separatist rebels, who have fought for an independent Tamil homeland in the island nation's north and east for more than two decades.

## Military Advances

The president's remarks come as government forces have reported significant territorial gains, including the recapture of Elephant Pass, a strategically vital land bridge connecting the northern Jaffna peninsula to the rest of the country. The narrow isthmus has long been considered a critical military chokepoint and a symbolic prize in the conflict.

Government officials have hailed the advances as evidence that the military campaign against the Tamil Tigers is entering its final phase, with the rebels increasingly confined to a shrinking area of territory.

## Press Freedom Concerns

Rajapaksa's conspiracy allegations arrive against a backdrop of mounting concern over press freedom in Sri Lanka. A series of attacks on journalists has drawn condemnation from international media watchdogs and human rights organizations, who accuse the government of fostering a climate of intolerance toward critical reporting.

Media rights groups have documented cases of journalists being threatened, assaulted, and in some instances killed. Critics argue that reporters covering the war and questioning official narratives have faced particular pressure.

The government has denied involvement in attacks on the press and has, at times, suggested that such incidents may themselves be part of efforts to discredit the administration.

## Humanitarian Questions

International observers have raised concerns about the humanitarian situation for civilians trapped in conflict zones, as well as the treatment of displaced Tamil populations. Aid organizations have called for greater access to affected areas and independent monitoring of conditions.

The Sri Lankan government has maintained that its military operations are aimed at liberating civilians from LTTE control and has rejected calls that it characterizes as interference in the country's internal affairs.

## A Divisive Conflict

The decades-long civil war has claimed tens of thousands of lives and remains one of Asia's most protracted armed conflicts. The Tamil Tigers, designated a terrorist organization by numerous countries, have been known for suicide bombings and the recruitment of child soldiers, while government forces have faced their own accusations of human rights violations.

As the military campaign continues, the divide between the government's portrayal of an imminent triumph and international calls for restraint and accountability appears to be widening.

*This is a developing story.*

---

*Note: This article is written in a general CNN news style based on the scenario provided. Readers seeking current, verified information should consult authoritative news sources and official reporting.*

**COLOMBO** — Sri Lankan military forces continued their offensive against Tamil Tiger rebels in the country's northern region this week, as President Mahinda Rajapaksa addressed the nation amid mounting international concern over civilian safety and press freedom in the conflict zone.

## President Addresses the Nation

In a televised address, President Rajapaksa declared that government forces were on the verge of a decisive victory against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), the separatist group that has fought for an independent Tamil homeland for more than a quarter century.

"We are entering the final chapter of this long struggle," the president told the nation, calling on remaining rebel fighters to lay down their arms. He urged the LTTE to allow civilians trapped in the shrinking conflict zone to move safely into government-controlled territory.

The president also appealed for national unity, emphasizing that the campaign was directed against terrorism rather than against the Tamil population. He pledged development and reconciliation efforts for the war-affected northern districts once fighting concluded.

## Fighting Intensifies in the North

Military officials reported significant territorial gains as troops pressed deeper into the last strongholds held by the rebels in the northeastern Vanni region. The army said it had captured key positions and continued to constrict the area under LTTE control to a narrow strip of land.

Independent verification of battlefield claims remained difficult, as journalists and aid organizations faced severe restrictions on access to the front lines. Humanitarian agencies expressed alarm over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians reportedly caught between advancing forces and entrenched rebel positions.

The United Nations and international relief groups called for the establishment of safe corridors and pauses in fighting to permit the evacuation of the wounded and the delivery of essential supplies. Reports emerged of overcrowded conditions and shortages of food and medicine within the conflict zone.

## Attacks on Media Raise Alarm

The period was marked by disturbing developments concerning press freedom. Media organizations and press freedom advocates condemned a series of attacks targeting journalists and news outlets critical of the government's handling of the war.

A prominent newspaper editor known for his critical coverage was killed in a targeted attack, prompting widespread condemnation both domestically and abroad. In separate incidents, a major broadcast studio was assaulted by armed groups, and other journalists reported receiving threats.

Press freedom organizations characterized the climate as increasingly hostile to independent reporting. Government officials denied involvement in the attacks and pledged investigations, but critics questioned the commitment of authorities to safeguarding journalists.

## Opposition and International Criticism

Opposition figures accused the government of using the war to suppress dissent and consolidate power. They charged that emergency regulations and a nationalistic atmosphere were being exploited to silence critics and intimidate the press.

Human rights organizations raised concerns about alleged violations by both sides in the conflict, including the rebels' reported use of civilians as human shields and the government's handling of displaced populations. International governments urged restraint and called for the protection of noncombatants.

Government spokesmen rejected accusations of wrongdoing, insisting that military operations were being conducted with concern for civilian welfare. Officials accused some international critics and media outlets of relying on rebel propaganda and failing to appreciate the threat posed by the insurgency.

## Looking Ahead

As the military campaign advanced, questions loomed over the humanitarian situation, the future of Sri Lanka's Tamil minority, and the prospects for lasting reconciliation. With the conflict appearing to approach a military conclusion, observers warned that the political challenges of healing a divided nation would prove no less formidable than the fighting itself.

The government maintained that victory over the LTTE would open the way to peace and development, while critics cautioned that a durable settlement would require addressing the underlying grievances that fueled decades of civil war.

---

*This report reflects developments during the early 2009 phase of the Sri Lankan civil war.*
